prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the mortgage-underwriting agent (residential mortgage applications and remortgages) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: illness affecting income. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a member says illness has reduced their hours or stopped overtime, I check the last three to six months of payslips against the usual pattern before I assume the income drop is permanent."},{"type":"fact","content":"When illness is temporary and there is a clear return-to-work date, I treat the case differently from a long-term reduction and only count the income that is reliably available now."},{"type":"observation","content":"When benefits or sick pay are being received, I verify how long they will continue, because a short remaining period can overstate affordability if I simply annualise the current amount."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the illness is affecting only one household income, I prefer to test affordability on the stronger single income first and then add any proven secondary income only if it is stable."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a member has variable pay, I look for a post-illness average rather than a historic peak, since older earnings may no longer reflect the current capacity to work."},{"type":"fact","content":"When medical leave is ongoing, I do not treat future anticipated earnings as usable unless there is documentary evidence of a confirmed return and revised pay level."},{"type":"observation","content":"When remortgaging, I check whether the requested term or monthly payment would still be manageable if illness-related income loss continues for the next few months."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the member provides employer confirmation, I give it more weight than verbal assurances, especially where the illness has led to reduced shifts, redeployment or adjusted duties."},{"type":"observation","content":"When illness has caused irregular attendance, I compare current income to essential outgoings rather than to the previous income alone, because affordability risk often shows up in cashflow first."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the evidence shows income has recovered and remained stable for several months, I can use the recovered amount for underwriting, but I still note the recent illness as a risk factor."}]}
